VJ software compared

VDMX vs TouchDesigner: which should you use?

By Syd Lawrence, a visual artist and developer who makes Vibresia. Facts last checked 2 November 2026; updated 2 November 2026.

Pick VDMX if you want a finished VJ application for live shows on a Mac, with layers, effects and MIDI, OSC and DMX control already built. Pick TouchDesigner if you want to build your own interactive or generative system from nodes, need Windows as well as macOS, or want to start free with the Non-Commercial licence. They also work together: VDMX6 Plus adds TouchDesigner integration, so you don't have to choose only one.

Pick TouchDesigner if

you want to build your own interactive installation, live visual system or generative piece from nodes, you need Windows as well as macOS, or you want to learn for free before paying for a Commercial licence.

Pick VDMX if

you're a VJ on a Mac who wants a finished app for live shows: layers, blend modes, effect chains and MIDI, OSC or DMX control, ready to use rather than built from scratch.

Where TouchDesigner wins

TouchDesigner is Derivative's node-based visual programming environment for real-time interactive media. You don't get a finished show when you open it. You get the parts to build one, and that is its strength: it can build almost anything, as long as you build it. It suits artists and developers building interactive installations, live visuals and generative work.

It's also the easier one to start with on cost. There is a free non-commercial licence for personal use and learning, priced at Free. That version is capped at 1280x1280 output and can't be used for paid work, but it lets you learn the whole way of working before you spend anything. VDMX has no free tier; its trial is fully functional except that it can't save projects.

TouchDesigner runs on Windows, Mac. If any part of your work happens on a Windows machine, that settles it, because VDMX is Mac only. Licences are perpetual, with a year of updates included.

Where VDMX wins

VDMX is Vidvox's modular VJ software for the Mac. The live-show tools are already there when you open it, so you spend your time on the show rather than on the system that runs it. Its feature list covers:

Compositing: Layer compositing with blend modes, masks and real-time FX chains.
Control: Control by MIDI, OSC and DMX, plus audio analysis, LFOs and step sequencers.
Shaders and plug-ins: ISF (GLSL) generators and effects, alongside FFGL and Vuo.
Getting video in and out: Inputs and outputs over Syphon and NDI, fullscreen displays and disk recording.

For a VJ, that list is most of a show. Audio analysis, LFOs and step sequencers are built in, and MIDI, OSC and DMX control lets you run the show from hardware or other software.

It also asks less of an older Mac. VDMX needs macOS 13 or later, Intel or Apple silicon. TouchDesigner on a Mac needs macOS 13 or later on a 2020-or-later Mac (Apple silicon highly recommended). And the paid version costs less: US$199.99 once for VDMX6, against US$600 for a TouchDesigner Commercial licence.

Where both fall short

Neither is free for paid work. TouchDesigner's free licence rules out paid projects and caps output at 1280x1280, and its Educational licence at US$300 rules out paid work too. VDMX's trial can't save a project, so you can try it but you can't run a real show from it without buying.

Neither is a quick start for someone who only wants something to look at. TouchDesigner gives you an environment to build in. VDMX gives you a full VJ rig, which still means loading clips, building layers and mapping controls before a show.

And on a Mac, both need macOS 13 or later. If your Mac can't run that, neither is an option.

What it costs, and using both

On their own, VDMX6 is US$199.99, one-time and TouchDesigner Commercial is US$600, one-time. TouchDesigner Pro, which adds Pro Support (6 hours), is US$2,200. TouchDesigner's prices are listed as "from", and its licences are perpetual with a year of updates included. Vidvox mentions educational, hobbyist and upgrade discounts for VDMX without giving amounts.

You don't have to pick only one. VDMX6 Plus, at US$349, adds Vuo and TouchDesigner integration, so you can bring TouchDesigner work into a VDMX setup. TouchDesigner is licensed separately, so for paid work the pair comes to US$949: VDMX6 Plus plus a TouchDesigner Commercial licence. If you're still learning, the free Non-Commercial licence brings that down to the price of VDMX6 Plus alone, within its 1280x1280 cap.

Questions people ask

Is VDMX or TouchDesigner better for VJing?

For a live VJ show on a Mac, VDMX gives you the tools ready-made: layers, blend modes, effect chains, and MIDI, OSC and DMX control. TouchDesigner can do live visuals too, but you build the system yourself in its node-based environment.

Can VDMX and TouchDesigner work together?

Yes. VDMX6 Plus adds Vuo and TouchDesigner integration. The plain VDMX6 licence doesn't include it, and TouchDesigner is licensed separately.

Is there a free version of VDMX or TouchDesigner?

TouchDesigner has a free Non-Commercial licence for personal use and learning, capped at 1280x1280 output and not for paid work. VDMX has no free tier, but its trial is fully functional except for saving projects.

Does VDMX run on Windows?

No. VDMX is Mac only, on macOS 13 or later with Intel or Apple silicon. TouchDesigner runs on both Windows and macOS.
